What we have built, in pictures

Every picture below was made by your own runs. Read each block as: what it is, an example of the data, what to look at, and what it tells us.

1Pick the important moments (Key States)

A match has about 58,000 frames. We keep only the frames where the pitch changed enough. Calm moments give few Key States, busy moments give many.

Real match: 58,387 frames, 3,550 kept (6%). Simulator: 3,000 frames, about 360 kept (12%).

Look at: the real match (top strip) flickers and has grey blocks (stoppages); the simulated strips are smooth, with almost no grey.

2Cut the match into scenes (sequences)

Where the shape of play changes, a new scene starts. Red lines are scene boundaries, grey shading is the ball not in play.

Real scene 34: 133 s, ball dead 0% (open play). Real scene 117: 52 s, ball dead 85% (a stoppage).

Look at: the red lines often sit at the start and end of the grey blocks, even though the method never saw the ball-dead flag.

3Two kinds of scene

Only two kinds of scene appear in every real match: open play and stoppage.

Real matches: 28 to 36% of scenes are stoppages. Simulator: 0 to 4.5%.
The simulator is almost all open play. Real football stops a lot.

4Turn each moment into a small network (graph)

22 players and the ball become dots. Grey lines join teammates, red lines join opponents within 8 m, orange lines join the ball to its nearest players.

Key State at 599.9 s: 23 dots, 70 teammate links, 10 opponent links, 3 ball links.

Look at: real (left) and simulated (right) look alike in a single picture. The difference shows up over time.

5Add time

Four moments in a row. Faded dots are where each player was, arrows show where they went.

Simulated players move about 2.3 times faster than real ones (median 3.4 vs 1.5 m/s).

6Group the network's summaries into tactical states

The network writes 48 numbers for each moment. Left: every moment is one dot (green real, orange simulated). Right: how much time each match spends in each kind of state.

State 1 (slow players, ball dead 80%): real 15 to 21%, simulator under 3%. State 4 (fast running): real about 30%, simulator 50 to 64%.
The network found a "waiting around" state by itself. The simulator hardly visits it.

7Which measure finds the important moments?

The test asks which measure points at "the ball goes dead or play restarts". Left: score for each measure (50 is a coin flip). Right: if you keep only the biggest jumps, how many of those moments you keep.

3 m rule 51%, time gap 79%, network 80%, hand-made group 82%, simple mix 84%, combined 85%.
Combining the network's "surprise" with the time gap works better than either one alone, in all 7 real matches.
